finding.title: Unset flags overwrite defaults with undefined

findings.title: Unset flags overwrite defaults with undefined
findings.scenario: Running the probe with no flags makes cli.js pass { baseUrl: undefined, retries: undefined, timeoutMs: undefined }. Spreading that over DEFAULTS sets every field to undefined. The URL becomes 'undefined/status'. The loop `attempt <= undefined` is false, so it never runs and get() throws undefined. AbortSignal.timeout(undefined) would also fail. The author wanted the defaults kept when a flag is not given, and this breaks that.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The spread copies own keys whose value is undefined. cli.js always sets all three keys, and no test covers the no-flag case.

findings.title: Non-numeric --retries/--timeout become NaN with no validation
findings.scenario: `--retries abc` gives NaN. `attempt <= NaN` is false, so no request is made and the probe throws undefined. `--timeout abc` gives NaN, and AbortSignal.timeout(NaN) throws. Both are user input and are not checked.
findings.whyNotPrevented: parseArgs returns strings and nothing checks that they are finite, non-negative numbers.

findings.title: Lock is never released on the missing-account path
findings.quote: throw new PayoutError(`payout ${payoutId} has no bank account`);
findings.scenario: A payout has no accountNumber. sendPayout acquires the lock, marks the payout failed, and throws before the try/finally. release() is never called, so the payout:<id> lock stays held. Any later call for that payout, such as a retry, waits on the lock forever. The same happens if payouts.get or payouts.update throws.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The try/finally starts after the new block, so release() only runs for code inside the try. No test covers this path.

findings.title: Missing-account check runs before the already-sent check
findings.scenario: A payout with status 'sent' but no accountNumber, for example because the account field was later cleared or archived, is overwritten with status 'failed'. Before this change the same call returned the sent payout unchanged.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The check comes before the idempotency check on status === 'sent'.

findings.whyNotPrevented: The missing-account check runs before the `status === 'sent'` idempotency check, and no test covers it.

findings.title: Refund transfer has its arguments reversed, so money moves from the customer to the store
findings.scenario: transfer's signature is (toAccountId, fromAccountId, amountCents). This call passes STORE_ACCOUNT as the destination and the customer as the source. Refunding a 5000 cent order debits the customer 5000 and credits the store 5000, which is the opposite of a refund. payouts.js calls transfer(seller.accountId, STORE_ACCOUNT, ...) in the correct order.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The arguments are plain strings and the code is untyped JS. No test covers refunds.
findings.measuredBy: Read src/ledger.js:9 `transfer(toAccountId, fromAccountId, amountCents)`; src/payouts.js:4 uses the correct order

findings.title: Refunds are not tracked, so an order can be refunded repeatedly beyond its total
findings.scenario: Support submits POST /refunds twice for a 5000 cent order, each time with amountCents 5000 (or 3000 and then 3000 as partial refunds). Both calls pass the check and the customer receives more than the order total.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The check compares only against the order total. Nothing records how much has already been refunded for the order.

findings.title: The order and its total come from the request body, and the route has no support authorization
findings.scenario: A caller sends order: {totalCents: 99999999, customerAccountId: 'attacker'} with a large amountCents. The refund check passes against the caller's own totalCents and pays out. Any caller can also reach the route, not just support.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The handler does not load the order from a store and has no role check. The only check is against the client-supplied total.

findings.title: Refund transfer arguments are reversed, so it charges the customer

findings.title: Out-of-order responses can overwrite newer results
findings.scenario: The user types 'sho', pauses, then types 'shoe'. If the 'sho' response arrives after the 'shoe' response, the list shows results for 'sho' while the input says 'shoe'. Clearing the input to under 2 characters renders [] immediately, but a slower in-flight response can then repopulate the list.
findings.whyNotPrevented: debounce only delays calls. It does not cancel or ignore in-flight requests, and nothing tracks which request is the latest.

findings.title: Pressing Enter no longer runs a search
findings.scenario: The user types one character and presses Enter. Before this change that searched. Now the submit is swallowed and nothing happens. The same applies if the user presses Enter within the 200ms debounce window. They have to wait for the timer, and one character never searches.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The submit handler only calls preventDefault and does not call the search. No test covers Enter.

findings.title: New 2-character minimum is not part of the request
findings.scenario: Single-character product queries, which worked on Enter before, now return an empty list with no message.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The author asked only for a debounce, and nothing documents or tests the minimum.

forbidden.title: Validly signed event without `data` throws and crashes the process

findings.title: Validly signed event without `data` throws and crashes the process
findings.scenario: The provider sends a correctly signed event that has no `data` field, such as another event type or a JSON `null` body. `event.data.shipmentId` or `event.type` throws a TypeError. The server's async request callback has no catch, so the unhandled rejection terminates the Node process, and the provider's retries could keep it down. The request also never gets a response.
findings.whyNotPrevented: Only the JSON syntax is validated. Nothing checks the event shape. `server.js` awaits the handler without try/catch. Non-ping event types are all treated as shipment updates.

other.title: Signed event with a missing data field throws, and nothing in the server catches it
Events for an unknown shipment are acknowledged with 200 and dropped

findings.title: Signed event with a missing data field throws, and nothing in the server catches it
findings.scenario: A correctly signed event whose type is not 'ping' and that has no `data` (or a body that parses to `null`) throws a TypeError. `startServer` does not catch errors from the handler, so the request gets no response. On Node 15 and later the unhandled rejection can also terminate the process. The provider retries until it gets a 2xx, so it keeps sending the same bad event.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The ShippingEvent typedef marks data as optional, and the handler does not check it. server.js has no try/catch around the handler call.

findings.title: Events for an unknown shipment are acknowledged with 200 and dropped
findings.scenario: The provider's event arrives before the shipment exists locally. `updateShipment` returns null, the handler still returns 200, and the provider stops retrying. The status update is lost.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The handler ignores the return value of `updateShipment`. Nothing in the change shows whether this case can happen, so this is a suspicion.

finding.title: Saved preferences are written into the shared defaults object, so they leak between users

other.title: `key in` also matches inherited keys such as constructor and __proto__

findings.title: Saved preferences are written into the shared defaults object, so they leak between users
findings.scenario: defaultPreferences() returns the module-level DEFAULT_PREFERENCES, not a copy. User A has saved theme 'dark'. Fetching A mutates the shared defaults. User B has no saved theme, but a later fetch of B returns theme 'dark'. Defaults are corrupted for every later request, and A's preferences are exposed to other users.
findings.whyNotPrevented: defaults.js returns the same object on every call, and the object is not frozen or copied. No test covers two users in sequence.
findings.measuredBy: Read src/defaults.js: `return DEFAULT_PREFERENCES;` returns the shared constant

findings.title: `key in` also matches inherited keys such as constructor and __proto__
findings.scenario: Saved JSON containing "constructor" or "toString" passes the `in` check, because `in` also looks at the prototype chain. The value then overwrites that property on the result, which is not a supported preference key. A saved "__proto__" key is a related case.
findings.whyNotPrevented: `in` checks the prototype chain. Nothing restricts keys to own properties.

finding.title: Mutates the shared defaults object, so one user's preferences leak into every other user

other.title: `in` operator also matches inherited keys such as constructor and __proto__

findings.title: Mutates the shared defaults object, so one user's preferences leak into every other user
findings.scenario: defaultPreferences() returns the module-level DEFAULT_PREFERENCES object, not a copy. User A has saved theme 'dark'. preferencesFor(A) writes 'dark' into the shared object. User B has no saved preferences. preferencesFor(B) then returns theme 'dark'. The global defaults are permanently changed for every later request.
findings.whyNotPrevented: DEFAULT_PREFERENCES is not frozen, defaultPreferences() does not copy it, and no test calls preferencesFor for two users in a row.
findings.measuredBy: Read src/defaults.js: defaultPreferences() returns the DEFAULT_PREFERENCES constant directly

findings.title: `in` operator also matches inherited keys such as constructor and __proto__
findings.scenario: Saved JSON such as {"constructor":"x"} or {"toString":1} passes the `in` check because those keys are inherited from Object.prototype. They are then written onto the preferences object and returned, even though they are not supported keys. A saved `__proto__` key from JSON.parse is an own property, so assigning it can change the prototype.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The check uses `in` instead of Object.hasOwn, and nothing validates the saved keys.

finding.title: Writes saved values into the shared DEFAULT_PREFERENCES object, leaking one user's preferences to others

other.title: `in` operator also matches inherited keys

findings.title: Writes saved values into the shared DEFAULT_PREFERENCES object, leaking one user's preferences to others
findings.scenario: User A has savedPreferences {theme:'dark'}. GET user A mutates the module-level DEFAULT_PREFERENCES, so theme becomes 'dark'. GET user B, who has no saved preferences, then returns theme 'dark' instead of 'light'. The defaults are permanently changed for the life of the process.
findings.whyNotPrevented: defaultPreferences() in src/defaults.js returns the DEFAULT_PREFERENCES constant itself, not a copy. Nothing freezes it, and no test covers two users in sequence.
findings.measuredBy: Read src/defaults.js: `return DEFAULT_PREFERENCES;` returns the module-level object. Read src/preferences.js: the loop assigns into that same object.

findings.title: `in` operator also matches inherited keys
findings.scenario: Saved JSON contains {"toString":"x"} or {"constructor":1}. `in` returns true for these inherited properties, so they are copied into the response as unsupported keys. A saved `__proto__` key is a related case, though JSON.parse makes it an own property and the assignment then changes the prototype.
findings.whyNotPrevented: `in` checks the prototype chain. Nothing restricts the allowed keys to own properties.
